# A Note on AI Assistance {.unnumbered}

Every chapter of this book was researched, written, and rewritten by me. I also used AI tools throughout. What follows is more than the disclosure MIT Press requires of authors who use AI. It is a statement of the standard I held the book to, and a claim about what authorship means when the tools act as both force-multiplier and tutor.

In my previous volumes, the systems and infrastructure domain was my native intellectual home. There, AI was a utility for writing code, auditing cross-references, and enforcing consistency. But *Physical AI* pushed me across the causal boundary into mechanical engineering, control barrier functions, and kinematic chains. Here, I had to be a student again. I used large language models as interactive tutors to trace derivations from classical control literature, explore unfamiliar dynamics, and pressure-test my understanding. Because I was synthesizing concepts outside my core expertise, I then relied heavily on external verification from human roboticists and control engineers to vet the architectures I developed.

The standard remains traceability. Derived quantities in these chapters are backed by Python computation cells whose source code ships with the book. Citations were checked against their sources. AI tools made a steep learning curve mechanically tractable. The enforcement infrastructure makes that work auditable.

Authorship is thinking. Which concepts belong in this book and which do not. How to sequence the chapters so that each idea arrives only after the reader has the tools to understand it. What level to pitch each explanation at. Where students will get stuck. These are judgment calls that no tool can make, because they require knowing the reader. The ideas were thought by me; the prose was often drafted, expanded, or worded by AI before being aggressively rewritten and verified. The choices are mine.

Machine learning systems can not be certified the way traditional logic can. That verification gap applies to AI-assisted authoring with equal force. The standard I held this book to is the standard I want us to demand of every physical system we ship: the tool can propose, and the tool can tutor, but only an engineer can ratify. MIT Press does not list AI tools as authors because they can not assume ethical and legal responsibility for their work. The same is true of every engineered system. Authorship is the assumption of that responsibility, and it belongs to the human.
